opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really interesting tension. On one hand, the field is young enough that someone can show up, spend six months going deep on a problem, and produce something that genuinely moves the frontier. There aren't decades of accumulated tacit knowledge you have to absorb before you're useful. A lot of what matters is taste, persistence, and a willingness to just run the experiment rather than theorize about it.

But on the other hand, I'd push back a bit on the idea that people are easily replaceable. What's hard to replace isn't raw knowledge. It's judgment built from having seen a lot of things fail. When you've watched dozens of runs blow up, or seen an idea that looked beautiful on paper fall apart at scale, you develop an intuition for where to spend your compute and attention. That's the scarce resource. Compute is constrained, so the person who can pick the right three experiments out of a hundred plausible ones is worth enormously more than someone who picks at random.

There's also the organizational piece. The people who are hardest to replace are often the ones who hold context across the whole stack: they understand the infrastructure, the data, the modeling, and how they interact. When something weird happens in a training run, they know where to look. That knowledge is surprisingly hard to write down, and it walks out the door with them.

So my take is that the barrier to *contributing* is low, which is wonderful and is why you see so many people break in quickly. The barrier to *being the person the effort hinges on* is much higher, and that's mostly about accumulated taste and context. The good news is that taste can be developed fast if you're in an environment with tight feedback loops and generous mentorship. That's probably the biggest lever labs have, more than hiring stars: building cultures where newcomers absorb that judgment as quickly as possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how hard key people are to replace, but does not distinguish team bus factor from the time needed to recover after losing them.

r002.rationale: It describes judgment learned from seeing many experiments fail and using that experience to choose where to spend compute and attention.

r003.rationale: It identifies hard-to-document context across the stack, but does not say that creating shared context around oneself is the particularly difficult skill.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing of "replacing key people" is slightly off, because it assumes the bottleneck is some fixed stock of irreplaceable talent. What I've actually seen is that the thing that matters most is engineering taste plus a willingness to run a huge number of experiments quickly, and that's learnable faster than people assume.

The reason newcomers can contribute so fast is that the field has an unusually short feedback loop. You have an idea, you implement it, you get a loss curve back in hours or days, and it tells you whether you were right. That's very different from, say, biology, where the experiment might take months and the apprenticeship period is correspondingly long. So in deep learning, someone who's smart, who's a strong engineer, and who's willing to just grind through the experiment loop can build real intuition in six months to a year. A lot of the people who've had outsized impact at the labs were, two years earlier, not obviously special on paper.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. There's a difference between contributing to a project and having the taste to pick which project matters. The people who are really hard to replace are the ones who can look at a messy pile of results and say "no, the thing we actually care about is over here," and then reorient a whole team around that. That kind of judgment comes from having burned through a lot of wrong ideas yourself. You can accelerate it, but you can't entirely skip it.

The other thing that gets underrated is that a lot of the apparent genius of key people is really context. They know why the last three attempts at some idea failed, they know which parts of the codebase are load-bearing, they know who to ask. When they leave, you lose the context more than you lose the raw ability. And context is replaceable, but only if the organization is deliberate about spreading it around rather than letting it pool in a few heads.

So my honest answer is: individual researchers are more replaceable than the mythology suggests, but research taste and institutional context are not, and the labs that do well are the ones that treat those as the scarce resources rather than headcount.

r001.rationale: The response discusses losing a key person’s context and how organizations can spread it, but does not distinguish team bus factor from recovery time after a loss.

r002.rationale: It describes rapid experiments as building intuition and says judgment comes from learning through many wrong ideas, characterizing research as learned empirical judgment.

r003.rationale: It identifies institutional context as important and says it must be deliberately spread, but does not identify the ability to create shared context around oneself as a particularly difficult skill to replace.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things that are easy to conflate. One is how quickly someone can make an important contribution, and the other is how quickly they can replace the judgment of someone who’s been doing this for years.

A newcomer can come in, notice something everyone else has missed, and get a result that changes what the team does. That’s part of what makes the field exciting. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they can look at twenty plausible research directions and pick the two that are worth spending the next six months on.

The really valuable people often do both: they have good ideas themselves, and they make everyone around them more effective. They can tell when a negative result means the idea is wrong versus when the experiment is broken. They know which assumptions you should question. And they help new people get to the point where they can contribute quickly.

So the fact that newcomers can be productive very quickly might actually be partly downstream of having those people around. You can’t necessarily remove the person who created that environment and assume the rate of new contributions stays the same. But equally, you shouldn’t conclude that the field depends on a fixed set of irreplaceable people. There’s a lot of talent that can develop surprisingly fast if you give it the opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response says removing a key person may reduce the rate of new contributions, but it does not distinguish a team’s bus factor from how long recovery after losing key people would take.

r002.rationale: It describes judgment built over years, including choosing promising directions and interpreting whether a negative result reflects a flawed idea or experiment.

r003.rationale: It says valuable researchers make others more effective and help newcomers develop, but does not clearly identify creating shared context around oneself as the especially difficult skill to replace.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things that can both be true. Someone can come into the field and, within six months, make a really important contribution. But that doesn’t mean you can reliably replace a particular person in six months. Finding the person who’s going to do that is a huge part of the difficulty.

And making an important contribution is different from repeatedly deciding what to work on. You can have a great idea, run an experiment, and get a really interesting result. The harder thing is having good judgment across a whole sequence of decisions: which results to trust, which directions to abandon, where to spend a lot of compute, and what’s worth getting other people excited about.

So I wouldn’t measure someone’s replaceability by how long it took them to become useful. The fact that they got up to speed incredibly quickly might itself be evidence that they’re quite unusual. You want to make it easy for newcomers to contribute, while recognizing that some people are extraordinarily good at turning that opportunity into progress.

r001.rationale: The response says a particular person cannot reliably be replaced in six months, but does not distinguish a team’s bus factor from its recovery time after losing key people.

r002.rationale: It describes judgment about experiments and research directions, but does not clearly say that deep learning research depends on empirical judgment learned through experience.

r003.rationale: The response mentions getting others excited about research, but does not identify creating shared context around oneself as a difficult skill to replace.
